newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks off lows at midday, look to jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks off lows at midday, look to jobs data.

text.p: U.S. stocks pushed off session lows by midday on Thursday, but financial markets remained somewhat jittery ahead of a key July employment report due out tomorrow, analysts said.
Stocks and bonds see-sawed for much of the morning, as investors sifted through a series of ambiguous economic data.
By midday, the Dow Jones Industrial average, which opened higher then slid, was off lows. It was down eight points at around 8246, keeping a mindful eye on the bond market.
The Nasdaq composite was up around two points at 1590.
The long bond recouped losses, gaining 3/32 to yield 6.32 percent.

"The market is waiting for tomorrow's employment number," Peter Coolidge, senior equity trader at Brean Murray & Co said. "The market has had a really decent run this week, with lots of positive momentum in both the credit and equity markets. But we are taking a little bit of a breather here."

The July employment data, due on Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, would draw intense market scrutiny because it offered clues about the third quarter, analysts said. The data has also shaken both bond and stock markets in the past.
"I expect the market to walk in place or even give back ground until we get information on the employment number," said Charles White, managing director at Avatar Associates.
The jobless rate was seen dipping to 4.9 percent, with non-farm payrolls rising by 193,000.
On Thursday, financial markets were also buffeted by second quarter gross domestic product data, weekly jobless claims and the Chicago Purchasing Managers report.
A benign 2.2 percent annualized rise in GDP during the second quarter, combined with a very small rise in the price deflator initially boosted stocks and bonds.
The deflator -- which showed its smallest gain since 1964 -- initially calmed the bond market's inflationary fears.
But markets tripped after a stronger-than-expected Chicago Purchasing Managers report.
The Chicago PMI read 60.6 in July, versus a forecast reading of 59.8. But analysts said the increase in its prices paid component was more disturbing to markets.

"The bond market in particular seemed to weaken after the Chicago PMI report and stocks followed suit," said Greg Nie, a technical analyst at EVEREN Securities. "Today's data was more on the confusing side than anything else."
Stocks also digested weekly jobless claims, which fell to 277,000 in the latest week and the help wanted ad index.
The Conference Board said its U.S. help wanted advertising index rose seven points in June to an 88.0 reading. The group said the U.S. labor market was expanding "about as fast as it possibly could."

Among particular issues, Wendy's International Inc stock slid 2-3/8 to 24-7/8. The restaurant company reported second quarter earnings of $0.42 per diluted share versus $0.38 per share in the year-ago quarter.

It also said its second half sales comparisons would be harder amid rising labor and raw material costs and a higher tax rate. Brokerage firms Merrill Lynch and Smith Barney both downgraded their ratings on the stock.
True North Communications Inc said it signed a definitive agreement to acquire Bozell, Jacobs, Kenyon and Eckhardt Inc in a deal valued at about $440 million.
Its stock rose 13/16 to 23-7/8.
((Wall Street desk 212-859-1730))
